sections.overview: The Eurasian magpie is a familiar corvid of Europe and much of northern and central Asia, recognizable by its black-and-white pattern and exceptionally long tail.
sections.identification: An adult is about 46–50 cm long and usually weighs 185–268 grams. More than half the bird’s length is tail, creating a striking silhouette in flight and on the ground. The head, back, and breast are black, with white belly, shoulder patches, and large white wing panels; juveniles are duller and have a shorter tail. In strong light, the dark wing and tail feathers flash blue and green: layers of hollow melanosomes in the feather barbules reflect light selectively, producing structural iridescence. A harsh, rattling chatter is its characteristic call.
sections.habitat: Magpies use farmland, villages, gardens, parks, open woodland, and the edges of towns. Trees and hedges provide nesting sites. They generally avoid dense forest, extensive wetlands, and treeless country, so the meeting of cover and open feeding ground matters more than any single habitat type.
sections.diet: This opportunistic omnivore searches mostly while walking or hopping over the ground, pausing to inspect likely prey before picking it up with its bill. Beetles and other invertebrates are important, alongside seeds, fruit, scraps, carrion, and occasionally eggs or nestlings; vertebrate food is usually a small share overall. A study of urban Manchester birds found a varied diet dominated by surface-dwelling invertebrates, with plant foods especially important in winter. Magpies also hide surplus food in small caches and retrieve it later, using nearby visual landmarks and other cues; some buried acorns are left behind and can germinate.
sections.behavior: Pairs usually defend a breeding territory, while young or nonbreeding birds may gather in family groups or communal roosts. Their harsh alarm chatter warns other magpies when cats and other predators are nearby. Magpies can store and relocate food, and experiments show that they use local cues to recover caches. The familiar tale that they are compelled to steal shiny trinkets is unsupported: captive and free-living birds in one experiment showed no unconditional preference for shiny objects and often hesitated around unfamiliar items. A 2008 mirror-mark experiment was interpreted as evidence of self-recognition. A larger 2020 replication did not confirm that result, so the test does not establish a universal capacity for self-awareness.
sections.reproduction: A pair builds a domed stick nest with a side entrance, usually in a tree; both sexes gather material, with the male bringing most and the female doing most construction. The female lays a typical clutch of five or six eggs and incubates them for about 20 days, while her mate supplies food. Chicks hatch naked and helpless, and both parents feed them. They usually fledge at about 26–31 days, then receive food from the adults for several more weeks. One brood is usual each year, and British records indicate that breeding commonly begins at about two years old.
sections.ecology: By taking eggs and nestlings, magpies can affect particular nests, especially when dependent fledglings increase the food demands of territorial adults. In a UK farmland study, artificial nests faced greater magpie predation inside breeding territories late in the season, but wider research has not found a simple national link between corvid increases and songbird declines. Their ecological role also includes seed dispersal: in western Mediterranean farmland, magpies carry and bury holm-oak acorns, and some caches produce seedlings. The balance between predation and seed movement therefore depends on local prey, habitat, and plant communities.
sections.conservation: The latest global IUCN assessment, published in 2024, classifies the Eurasian Magpie as Least Concern. That category does not rule out declines in particular local populations. In Britain, the BTO reports a 104% increase in the monitored population index between 1967 and 2024, alongside a 6.4% expansion in breeding distribution. Magpies have also been culled in British game management; a 2022 review documents this history and notes that control policies differ among UK nations. Evidence does not support treating magpies as a general cause of songbird decline; habitat change and food availability also shape those populations.
